ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.contribution: Mandatory first-year academic writing, source evaluation, research questions, reflection and community collaboration.

BENECON111.name: Introduction to Economics
BENECON111.contribution: Complementary microeconomic choice, markets, strategic interaction and macroeconomic foundations for analysing institutions and economic conditions behind inequality.

BENECON211.name: International Macroeconomics
BENECON211.contribution: Complementary open-economy growth, labour-market and fiscal/monetary analysis for the economic structures connecting societies; not dedicated migration studies.

BENECON311.name: Public Economics
BENECON311.contribution: Direct distributive and institutional policy analysis through public goods, externalities, taxation, public spending, welfare, education and health, with economic evidence and a research paper.

BENECON312.name: Econometrics
BENECON312.contribution: Direct regression, causal/predictive inference, OLS/GLS/IV and statistical testing in Stata, with Monte Carlo simulations and an empirical paper; economic applications rather than a sociology methods duplicate.

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.contribution: Direct empirical research design, operationalisation, survey/experimental methods, inference and regression, including original team data collection and ethical reporting.

BENLEAD211.name: Psychology of Leading Under Pressure
BENLEAD211.contribution: Direct study of psychological safety, belonging, minority experiences and inclusive leadership, with original supervised survey data and statistical reporting; not a complete sociology of education/work.

DISDATA111.name: Introduction to Data Science
DISDATA111.contribution: Direct R data cleaning, visualisation and tabular/text/spatial analysis with a student research question; no unsupported social-network-analysis specialisation.

ENSDELT312.name: Governance of Sustainability
ENSDELT312.contribution: Direct collective-action, institutions, power, justice, stakeholder and governance analysis of sustainability problems, with policy advice/evaluation.

GOSGATE102.name: Law, Society & Justice
GOSGATE102.contribution: Direct socio-legal study of law, social control/change and justice with race/gender, institutional cases and a small research proposal.

GOSHIST112.name: Histories of Gender
GOSHIST112.contribution: Direct intersectional gender/sexuality history in North America, including racialised power, queer lives, oral history and community-engaged research.

GOSHIST211.name: History of Empires
GOSHIST211.contribution: Direct comparative imperial histories, legitimacy, economic systems, culture and colonial legacies, with independently developed historical inquiry; complementary to contemporary global sociology.

GOSHIST311.name: Native American Histories
GOSHIST311.contribution: Direct Indigenous history of colonial institutions, family separation, gendered violence, cultural resistance and reciprocity through collaborative public-history inquiry.

GOSHIST312.name: Researching the “American Century”
GOSHIST312.contribution: Direct research-question development, critical source inquiry, interdisciplinary method and a substantial historical paper in Researching the American Century; not the excluded historical Walcheren outline.

GOSLAWJ111.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
GOSLAWJ111.contribution: Complementary legal/philosophical human-rights arguments, universalism, statelessness and rights protection for evaluating unequal power and inclusion.

GOSLAWJ212.name: Introduction to Public International Law
GOSLAWJ212.contribution: Complementary international-law institutions, self-determination, rights and treaty politics for analysing global legal relations; not a dedicated citizenship/integration course.

GOSLAWJ213.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
GOSLAWJ213.contribution: Complementary comparative constitutional/administrative analysis of power, rights, participation and remedies in public institutions.

GOSLAWJ311.name: Principles of Private Law
GOSLAWJ311.contribution: Complementary property, tort, contract and dispute-resolution analysis of rights and obligations in everyday private relations; no claimed family/housing specialisation.

GOSPOLI112.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
GOSPOLI112.contribution: Direct comparative analysis of political institutions, participation, populism, democracy and inequality-relevant political economy, with empirical research.

GOSPOLI212.name: Theory of International Relations
GOSPOLI212.contribution: Complementary IR theories, colonial relations, North–South economic connections and global political cases, with researched international negotiation.

GOSPOLI311.name: European Union Politics
GOSPOLI311.contribution: Direct EU institutions, interest representation and policy processes, including empirical amendment coding and legislative research.

GOSPOLI312.name: Public Policy Analysis
GOSPOLI312.contribution: Direct public-policy phases and alternative conceptualisations across national/international arenas through a global sugar case and policy memos.

GOSPOLI313.name: Peace & Conflict
GOSPOLI313.contribution: Direct interdisciplinary study of structural inequality, identity, colonial legacies, forced migration and conflict, with evidence-based policy research and positionality reflection.

GOSSOCI111.name: Introduction to Sociology
GOSSOCI111.contribution: Direct sociological imagination, classical theories, institutions, social boundaries, class/race/gender, migration and work/education inequalities; theory-led literature research.

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.contribution: Direct qualitative design, interviews, observation, reflexivity, coding and thematic interpretation, with original team research; mixed-method foundations do not equal a dedicated integration course.

GOSSOCI214.name: Modern Sociology
GOSSOCI214.contribution: Direct critical and modern social theories, Frankfurt School, Black feminism, Bourdieu, coloniality and empirical sociological interpretation.

GOSSOCI215.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
GOSSOCI215.contribution: Direct social-movement theories and environmental-justice cases with feminist, anticolonial, degrowth and environmental-peacebuilding perspectives.

GOSSOCI311.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
GOSSOCI311.contribution: Direct civil-society theory through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial approaches, trust, solidarity, movements and public spheres, applied in a research project.

HCBBIOM111.name: Epidemiology & Public Health
HCBBIOM111.contribution: Direct population-health evidence, social/environmental determinants, health inequalities, epidemiological methods and a local needs-assessment/intervention project.

HCBPSYC111.name: Social Psychology
HCBPSYC111.contribution: Complementary group processes, social cognition, prejudice and social influence for understanding interaction and identity; the final project proposes rather than executes a study.

HCBPSYC211.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
HCBPSYC211.contribution: Direct experimental design and multivariable statistical analysis, diagnostics, R/SPSS practice and empirical reporting for social/behavioural evidence.

HCBPSYC315.name: Youth Resilience to Extremism
HCBPSYC315.contribution: Direct educational inclusion, school belonging, youth radicalisation and civic agency through evidence-based teacher/youth resources and recipient feedback; not a general migration/political-psychology curriculum.

MCCCOMM212.name: Communicating the Climate Crisis
MCCCOMM212.contribution: Direct study of contested climate communication across public texts/media/protest art and arguments, with a project entering the debate.

MCCCOMM311.name: Persuasive Communication
MCCCOMM311.contribution: Direct ethical persuasion, framing and community sustainability communication, with literature, field diaries and reflective action research.

MCCHEAM212.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
MCCHEAM212.contribution: Complementary specific Renaissance Mediterranean art study of trade, colonisation and cross-cultural production connecting Europe, Africa, Asia and the Americas; not general migration training.

MCCMEDI311.name: Media & Race
MCCMEDI311.contribution: Direct study of racial construction, power, exclusion and resistance in American media/culture, with archival, participant-observation, podcast and cross-cultural narrative inquiry.

alignment.rationale: Both develop critical academic reading, arguments, reflection and study practice. UvA specifically trains the sociological imagination and analysis of sociological texts; UCR also develops writing and community collaboration.
Both develop software-based multiple-regression analysis and interpretation of evidence. UCR additionally treats econometric estimators, simulation, causal inference and an empirical economic paper.

Both develop research questions, operationalisation, survey methods and standards for empirical inquiry. UCR combines this with statistics and a team data project; UvA feeds its survey evidence into the subsequent statistics course.

Both examine unequal experiences and inclusion in organisations and working life. UCR develops psychological safety and minority inclusion through leadership and original survey research; UvA additionally centres schooling and the reproduction of educational and labour-market inequality.

Both examine institutions, social control and change through power and social relations. UCR centres law and justice; UvA more widely studies legitimacy, institutional reproduction and crisis across organisations.

Both connect global cultural and institutional relations to colonial power and its legacies. UCR approaches these through comparative imperial history; UvA directly studies contemporary cultural globalisation and transnational resistance.

Both develop research questions, critical reading and an independently argued academic paper. UCR works through historical sources and a substantial American Century research paper; UvA specifically develops sociological literature-review and writing skills.

Both examine policy formation, institutions, competing interests and how public problems are framed across national and international settings. UCR uses a global sugar case and policy memos; UvA studies sociological explanations across several policy fields.

Both introduce sociological concepts, social institutions, inequality and the analysis of contemporary problems through theory and research. The UvA component is larger and explicitly develops its Netherlands-focused and cross-cultural introduction.

Both develop qualitative coding, reflexivity, thematic interpretation and reporting. UCR additionally follows design and data collection through a team project; UvA explicitly includes thematic and discourse-analysis inquiry.
Both study critical sociological theory, including Marxist and Frankfurt School traditions. UCR additionally foregrounds modernity, colonialism, Black feminism and other theoretical approaches.

Both use contrasting social theories to examine social action, institutions and inequality. UCR concentrates on civil society, solidarity, public spheres and movements; UvA more broadly compares macro–micro explanations across work, education and households.

Both study population health, social determinants, health inequalities and empirical evidence. UCR adds epidemiological risk, study designs and a local public-health project; UvA centres sociological explanations and comparisons.

Both develop statistical inference, software analysis and empirical reporting. UCR extends into multivariable and experimental models; UvA introduces these statistical foundations through its earlier sociological survey data.

Both examine racialised power, intersecting identities, oppression and resistance. UCR centres American media and cultural history; UvA systematically connects race, gender and sexuality to epistemology, political economy and contemporary fascist forces.

Classical and contemporary theory also runs through the UCR sociology courses, but no additional selected course is counted as UvA’s distinct first theoretical foundation in interaction and social order.
No selected course develops the dedicated evolutionary and complexity account of cultural change, cooperation and human social organisation.
Research ethics and reflexivity occur elsewhere, but no selected course develops this distinct survey of social-science epistemology, ontology and philosophy.

UCR’s qualitative course includes interviewing, observation and a team project and is placed with qualitative analysis. No additional selected course is counted as this separately assessed introductory Amsterdam field project.

Migration and solidarity appear in sociology, conflict and global-relations courses. No selected course supplies the sustained migration, citizenship and integration theory and evidence of this dedicated component.
Social inequality, institutions and place recur in the alternatives, but no selected course centres urban social theory and urban inequality as this component does.
Modern Sociology includes Bourdieu and related work, but no additional selected course centres the dedicated culture–structure theoretical debate.
This thirty-credit elective space remains genuinely open, subject to the entry and registration conditions of the eventual choices.

Quantitative and qualitative inquiry are both available at UCR, including mixed-method foundations, but no selected course specifically develops their epistemological and analytical integration at this depth.

UCR includes several supervised research and writing projects, but no scheduled course supplies this individual eighteen-credit sociological thesis. Optional independent research remains additional to the scheduled programme.

analysis: The strongest feasible response is a substantial sociology core, not merely general social-science breadth. All five available Sociology courses develop classical, modern/critical and contemporary civil-society theory, qualitative inquiry and social movements. The closest adds quantitative design, experimental/multivariable statistics, econometrics and data handling, health inequality, historical method, institutional/policy and organisational inquiry. This materially responds to defining UvA theory, inequality and empirical sociology while preserving dedicated gaps.

Thirty-six actual UCR course contributions were assessed against current151active rows. Description-only Public Policy Analysis, Econometrics, Social Movements, Climate Communication, American Century historical inquiry and Mediterranean art connections receive their actual stated scope. No missing profile is reconstructed. GOSHIST312 uses the current description only, excluding Walcheren. Course identities/names are updated from the workbook, including Leading Under Pressure and American Century.

Three purposeful course changes: closest Peace/Conflict becomes Public Policy Analysis to strengthen actual policy-process content; institutional consumer-product design becomes Public Economics to examine distribution, public goods, taxation and social expenditure; global partner-dependent sustainability research becomes Public Policy Analysis for global/social-policy processes. Retained Peace/Conflict in the other two options has real structural-inequality, identity, colonial/forced-migration and policy-research substance. Youth Resilience is bounded to inclusive schools, youth belonging and prevention-resource work. Mediterranean art is specific cultural-production/exchange evidence, not broad migration training.

Four original offering conflicts are repaired using currentterm X values, with no restored offerings. All plans have24unique courses/180credits,4percoveredterm, first-yearPPD, formal prerequisites earlier and at least6advanced courses. Introductory sociology precedes modern/advanced theory; the available advisory progression is respected without inventing hard constraints. BENECON111 must be in2026h2; PublicEconomics is planned2028h1 and follows methods; global sustainability research is removed rather than assigned an unsupported2028h1 offering.

Pairwise course sets differ by52.5,52.5and60credits each way, with real differences in statistical/health research, institutional/legal/distributive policy and imperial/Indigenous/gender/global relations. Each direction has a coherent substantive purpose and enough supported distinct courses; inclusion stops at the maximum only after both candidates pass.

Fifteen supported partial relationships and ten additional gaps cover25external components and36UCRcourses once. IntroductiontoSociology is paired to the larger introduction, ModernSociology to CriticalTheory, contemporary civil-society theory to Theory3 with explicit limits. PublicPolicyAnalysis now supplies a concrete policy-process relationship. LeadingUnderPressure provides organisational inclusion/research, not the full education/work field; LawGate supplies a socio-legal institutional strand, not all institutionalcrisis sociology. HistEmpires supports colonial cultural-globalisation partly, not identical contemporary study.

Quantitative and qualitative strengths are fairly counted: R/experimental statistics, econometrics, original survey project and interviews/coding are reviewed. No full UvA18-credit thesis is inferred from the sustainability partner project or another smaller course; optional15-credit UCR independent research stays additional to scheduled180. Dedicated evolutionary/complexity history, social-science philosophy, Amsterdam field-project assessment, migration/citizenship, urban sociology, culture/structure, mixed-method integration and open elective space remain visible. Gaps explain where related content is already counted rather than applying a false one-to-one equivalence test.
